name: How to Read a Savings Claim
title: How to Read a Savings Claim
answer: How to read a savings claim is the practice of separating a verified saving from a vendor promise. A verified saving is measured against a clear baseline, over a meaningful period, with the costs of the new tool included. This matters because boards can reinvest verified savings in students, while promised savings cannot be relied on.

sections.body: Vendors of operations tools often promise dramatic savings, and boards need a way to evaluate those claims. A verified saving compares what was spent before with what is spent now, using a clear baseline and a meaningful period, and it includes the new tool's license, training, and staff time. A promise is only a projection that has not yet been tested in the district. The problem is that a board may treat a projection as real money and decide on assurances rather than data. This idea gives boards questions to separate verified savings from promises.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The text gives no grade bands for this idea, so the practice applies to board and district decision making rather than a specific classroom level. Boards ask what was spent before and how it was measured, what is spent now including license, training, and staff time, and whether other changes such as falling enrollment or new staff explain the difference. They also check for hidden costs, such as a routing change that saves money but lengthens rides for students with disabilities, or an energy change that saves money but makes classrooms too cold. Boards ask who bears the costs of any savings. Figure 19.4 lists questions boards can ask about any savings claim, and the answers should come with data, not assurances.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text does not offer a research study or an evidence label for this idea, so it rests on practice rather than research. Its only supporting item is Figure 19.4, which lists questions boards can ask about any savings claim. The text states that answers should come with data, not assurances, and that a vendor or staff member who cannot answer the questions has not yet shown a verified saving.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are that a saving can hide costs outside the budget, so a lower number is not automatically a good outcome. A routing change that saves money but lengthens rides for students with disabilities carries a cost to those students. An energy change that saves money but makes classrooms too cold carries a cost to learning. Boards should ask who bears the costs of any savings. The decision to accept or reject a claim stays with the board, and it should rest on data rather than assurances.
